title: About
text: Welcome! I’m a Research Fellow at the University of Auckland, working at the intersection of population genomics and microbial ecology. See my CV for the full record, or my Research page for publications and citation metrics.

title: About
text:
Background
I did my PhD at the University of Otago, in Dunedin, New Zealand, focused on seaweed population genomics and microbiome structure. Before that, I completed a Master of Natural Science (Distinction) and Bachelor of Natural Science at Massey University, both specialising in molecular ecology. I now work as a Research Fellow at the University of Auckland, having previously been an Assistant Research Fellow and Lab Manager at the University of Otago.

title: About
text:
Research
I am a broadly trained molecular and microbial ecologist with principal expertise in population genomics and microbial ecology. I specialise in developing eco-evolutionary simulations of microbial communities to develop hypotheses which I then test using observational data and experiments.
My research background is a combination of population genomics and microbial ecology, with my current research interests working to align these two fields to understand the evolution of host-microbe relationships. My current work combines eco-evolutionary modelling of holobiont evolution, and experimental work with Daphnia to determine microbial contributions to host fitness and to understand host-microbial responses to environmental perturbations. In addition to these areas, I am also actively involved in the application and optimisation of new molecular biology protocols for non-model organisms.
More than anything, I like solving problems. Most of my work to date has been focussed on interesting questions, or tricky problems - like why some species don’t sequence so well with nanopore sequencing.

title: Projects
text:
During my PhD I struggled with Nanopore sequencing of seaweeds - an issue that turned out to be widespread in macroalgal genomics. Working with Nick Green in Chemistry at Otago, we used LC-MS on our DNA extracts and found strong evidence for polyphenol-DNA adducts causing rapid pore blocking and reduced sequencing yield, particularly in dried tissue. The findings have implications for genomic resource generation from macroalgae, including long-read sequencing of herbarium specimens.
Published as: A cry for kelp: Evidence for polyphenolic inhibition of Oxford Nanopore sequencing of brown algae, Journal of Phycology (2024).

title: Projects
text:
Seaweed Microbiome Biogeography
Work on the structure and biogeography of macroalgal (seaweed) microbiomes - looking at how host population dynamics, dispersal, and environmental drivers shape the microbial communities associated with kelp and other macroalgae across their range.
Published as: Macroalgal microbiome biogeography is shaped by environmental drivers rather than geographical distance, Annals of Botany (2024), and related work on host dispersal and rafting microbiomes in Nature Communications (2024).

title: Projects
section: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium Filtering for RADseq Data
text:
Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium Filtering for RADseq Data
A methods project investigating how commonly used Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium filtering schemes affect population structure inferences drawn from RADseq (reduced-representation sequencing) data - relevant to anyone using these filters as a standard QC step in population genomics pipelines.
Published as: Commonly used Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium filtering schemes impact population structure inferences using RADseq data, Molecular Ecology Resources (2022).

title: Projects
section: Mitogenomics and Biogeography of Isocladus armatus
text:
Mitogenomics and Biogeography of Isocladus armatus
The bulk of my Master’s research, on the New Zealand endemic marine isopod Isocladus armatus. First, I generated a mitogenome for this colour-polymorphic isopod and found it had a bizarre structure - an inverted, duplicated arrangement rather than the typical small circular mitogenome. Alongside this, I used genotyping-by-sequencing to study the species’ biogeography, finding strong population structure and isolation-by-distance, with the geographic arrangement of populations concordant with the genetic PCA space.
Published as: Long-read sequencing reveals atypical mitochondrial genome structure in a New Zealand marine isopod, Royal Society Open Science (2022), and Concordant geographic and genetic structure revealed by genotyping-by-sequencing in a New Zealand marine isopod, Ecology and Evolution (2020).

title: Projects
text:
Holobiont Eco-Evolutionary Simulations
Ongoing work developing eco-evolutionary simulations of microbial communities within hosts, to build and test hypotheses about holobiont (host-microbiome unit) evolution - in particular, how environmental variability shapes selection for microbiome-mediated host adaptation. This modelling work pairs with experimental work in Daphnia to test microbial contributions to host fitness under environmental change.
Published as: Within-host microbial selection and multiple microbial generations buffer the loss of host fitness under environmental change, FEMS Microbiology Ecology (2025).

See the Research page for the full publication list.

title: William Pearman
text:
I’m William Pearman - at the moment I am a Research Fellow at the University of Auckland, working on host-microbe evolution questions, using simulations. However more broadly I am a molecular ecologist, working on a range of projects from whole genome sequencing and population genomics, eDNA, microbial ecology, and nanopore sequencing of recalcitrant species.
My research background is a combination of population genomics and microbial ecology, and thus my current research interests are in aligning these two fields to understand the evolution of ‘holobionts’ or host-microbiome units. At present, I use eco-evolutionary modelling to develop frameworks and hypotheses regarding holobiont evolution which can then be tested using existing datasets. In particular, my current research aims to understand how environmental variability shapes selection and evolution of host-microbe systems, whereby higher levels of environmental variability may result in increased selection for microbiome-mediated adaptation of the host. In addition to these areas, I am also actively involved in the application and optimisation of new molecular biology protocols for non-model organisms.
More than anything, I like solving problems. Most of my work to date has been focussed on interesting questions, or tricky problems - like why some species don’t sequence so well with nanopore sequencing.
Feel free to get in touch if you want a copy of any of my publications, or if you’re interested in collaborating. See my CV for full details, or my Research page for publications and citation metrics.
